gloss: Egypt, the Egyptians; Mizraim; (root uncertain: perhaps “border, bounded land”)
summary: מִצְרַיִם is Egypt: Mizraim the son of Ham, the land named after him, and its people, who weep, flee and speak as one man (Gen 10:6; 50:3; Exo 14:25). Above all it is “the house of slaves” Yahweh brought Israel out of, the act by which he names himself and grounds his law and feasts, booths among them (Exo 20:2; Lev 23:43); its gentilic מִצְרִי is “Egyptian”, and the poets use the shorter מָצוֹר. The name is shared by every Semitic language that knew Egypt (Akkadian Muṣur, Ugaritic mṣrm, Arabic Miṣr), and Arabic and Akkadian also have a word miṣr, miṣru “boundary, territory” which may be its root; scripture itself never explains the name.

words.gloss: Egypt; the Egyptians; Mizraim son of Ham
words.summary: About 680 times. It names a man, his land and his people alike, as the names of nations do in Gen 10. Its ending is the ending of a dual (as in יָדַיִם), and it may once have meant a land in two parts; scripture never says so, but it names Pathros, the south, beside מִצְרַיִם as a separate land (Isa 11:11) as well as inside it (Jer 44:1, 15), and calls Pathros the land Egypt came from (Ezk 29:14). How the name comes from a root מצר is not shown by scripture: the cognates’ words for “boundary, territory” are the likeliest lead, recorded as possible.

senses.gloss: Mizraim, son of Ham, father of peoples
senses.definition: The second son of Ham, from whom came the Ludim, Pathrusim, Casluhim (whence the Philistines) and others: the ancestor whose name the land and nation bear. The psalms call Egypt “the land of Ham”.

evidence.note: “The sons of Ham: Cush and מִצְרַיִם and Put and Canaan.”
“And מִצְרַיִם fathered Ludim … and Pathrusim and Casluhim, from whom the Philistines came out.”
“Israel came into מִצְרַיִם, and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham.”
The firstborn struck “in מִצְרַיִם”, “in the tents of Ham”.

senses.definition: The land of the Nile south-west of Canaan, watered by its river, a refuge in famine, whose wadi marks the southern edge of Israel’s land. Usually אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם or plain מִצְרַיִם, often with the ending of direction מִצְרַיְמָה “to Egypt”.

evidence.note: Famine in the land, “and Abram went down to מִצְרַיְמָה to sojourn there.”
The Jordan plain was well watered “like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of מִצְרַיִם”.
The land Israel goes to possess “is not like the land of מִצְרַיִם … where you sowed your seed and watered it with your foot”.
The border runs from Azmon “to the wadi of מִצְרַיִם”.
The land promised to Abram “from the river of מִצְרַיִם to the great river, the river Euphrates”.
Jews “living in the land of מִצְרַיִם”, at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and in the land of Pathros.
“A famine came on all the land of Αἴγυπτος and Canaan.”

senses.gloss: the Egyptians, Egypt as a people
senses.definition: The nation of Egypt acting as one, with plural verbs or as a single speaker: mourning, pursuing, fleeing, and in the prophets coming to know Yahweh.

evidence.note: “And מִצְרַיִם wept (plural) for him seventy days.”
“And behold, מִצְרַיִם was marching after them.”
“And מִצְרַיִם said, Let me flee from before Israel, for Yahweh fights for them against מִצְרַיִם.”
“And מִצְרַיִם will know (plural) Yahweh in that day.”
“The family of מִצְרַיִם”.
“מִצְרַיִם is a very beautiful heifer.”

senses.gloss: the house of slavery Israel was brought out of
senses.definition: Egypt as the place of Israel’s bondage and of Yahweh’s redemption: “the land of Egypt, the house of slaves”, “the iron furnace”, from which he brought them out to be his people. The formula “who brought you out of the land of Egypt” is how Yahweh names himself to Israel.

evidence.note: “I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of מִצְרַיִם, out of the house of slaves.”
“Yahweh took you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of מִצְרַיִם, to be a people of inheritance to him.”
Brought out of the land of מִצְרַיִם “from being their slaves; and I broke the bars of your yoke”.
The booths kept so that the generations know “that I made the sons of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of מִצְרַיִם”.
“They are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of מִצְרַיִם; they shall not be sold as slaves are sold.”
“Out of מִצְרַיִם I called my son.”
Hos 11:1 quoted of Jesus brought back from Αἴγυπτος.
Jer 31:32: the day he took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Αἴγυπτος.

senses.gloss: Egypt as the help Israel trusts instead of Yahweh; the way back into bondage
senses.definition: In the law and the prophets Egypt is the power Israel turns to for horses and protection instead of Yahweh, a reed that breaks in the hand, and going back to Egypt is the undoing of the exodus, threatened as a curse.

evidence.note: “מִצְרַיִם is man and not God (אֵל), and their horses flesh and not spirit.”
Going down to מִצְרַיִם without asking Yahweh, to take refuge in its shadow, which becomes shame.
“You trust on this staff of a crushed reed, on מִצְרַיִם.”
The king must not make the people return to מִצְרַיְמָה to multiply horses: “you shall not go back that way again.”
The last curse: Yahweh will bring you back to מִצְרַיִם in ships.
Ephraim like a silly dove: “they call to מִצְרַיִם, they go to Assyria.”
“They shall return to מִצְרַיִם.”
The fathers “in their hearts turned back to Αἴγυπτος”.

evidence.locator: מִצְרַיִם → Αἴγυπτος ×509, Αἰγύπτιος ×90 (lemma count, MACULA alignment); Lev.23.43, מִצְרָיִם → αἰγύπτου; Hos.11.1, מִּצְרַיִם → αἰγύπτου

evidence.note: “Out of Αἴγυπτος I called my son” (Hos 11:1).
Moses counted the reproach of the Christ greater riches than the treasures of Αἴγυπτος, and by faith left it.
The Lord saved the people out of the land of Αἴγυπτος and afterwards destroyed those who did not believe.
The great city “which spiritually is called Sodom and Αἴγυπτος, where also our Lord was crucified”.

parallels.note: Egypt and Assyria, the two powers on either side, paired in Israel’s straying, its scattering and its regathering, and in Isaiah’s blessing of all three together.
Egypt as the land and tents of Ham, its father’s father.
The house of slaves, in apposition to the land of Egypt.
The iron furnace, set beside Egypt.

opposites.note: “Egypt is man and not God”: its help set against Yahweh’s.

phrases.gloss: bring out of the land of Egypt: the deliverance by which Yahweh names himself
the wadi of Egypt, the southern bound of Israel’s land

evidence.note: שְׁחִין מִצְרַיִם, the boil of Egypt.

words.summary: The gentilic of מִצְרַיִם: a man or woman of Egypt (feminine מִצְרִית, plural מִצְרִים, מִצְרִיּוֹת). The database files most of the tokens of מִצְרַיִם under this key as well; its own forms are about thirty.

senses.definition: A person of Egypt, named as such where it matters to the story: Hagar the Egyptian, Potiphar, the man Moses struck, the Egyptian slave in David’s hands; and the Egyptians as a people, who would not eat with Hebrews and who oppressed Israel.

evidence.note: “She had a שִׁפְחָה מִצְרִית, and her name was Hagar.”
Potiphar, Pharaoh’s officer, “an אִישׁ מִצְרִי”.
Moses “saw an אִישׁ מִצְרִי striking a Hebrew man”.
The Hebrew women are “not like the Egyptian women (הַמִּצְרִיֹּת)”.
“The Egyptians (הַמִּצְרִים) could not eat bread with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to מִצְרַיִם.”
“The Egyptians dealt ill with us and afflicted us.”
The son of an Israelite woman and an אִישׁ מִצְרִי.
Moses struck down the Αἰγύπτιος.

senses.definition: The law sets the Egyptian apart from the nations Israel must not marry or admit: he is not to be abhorred, because Israel was a sojourner in his land, and his children of the third generation may enter Yahweh’s assembly. Ezra later lists the Egyptian among the peoples whose abominations Israel had not separated from.

evidence.note: “You shall not abhor a מִצְרִי, for you were a sojourner in his land.”

evidence.locator: מִצְרִי → Αἰγύπτιος ×24 (lemma count, MACULA alignment); Gen.39.1 and Exo.2.11, מִצְרִי → αἰγύπτιος, αἰγύπτιον

evidence.note: Moses was taught in all the wisdom of the Αἰγύπτιοι.
The Αἰγύπτιοι, trying the Red Sea, were drowned.

words.summary: A shorter name of Egypt in poetry and prophecy, without the dual-like ending, the same in form as Akkadian Muṣur. It is spelled like מָצוֹר “siege, fortification” of צור, and the database tags all fourteen tokens of that spelling under both keys; only the five below are Egypt. Mic 7:12 could be read “the fortified cities”, but its pairing with Assyria and the River favours Egypt.

senses.definition: Egypt named for its Nile channels and its cities, beside Assyria and the River.

evidence.note: In the burden of מִצְרַיִם (19:1): “the Nile-streams (יְאֹרֵי) of מָצוֹר will dwindle and dry up; reed and rush will wither.”
Sennacherib boasts: “with the sole of my feet I dried up all the Nile-streams of מָצוֹר.”
“From Assyria and the cities of מָצוֹר, and from מָצוֹר to the River.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s Egypt (ܡܨܪܝܢ), with the Aramaic ending -ēn where Hebrew has -ayim, everywhere the Greek has Αἴγυπτος. SEDRA files it under its own root.

senses.definition: The land of Joseph and of Israel’s bondage, and the refuge of the child Jesus.

evidence.note: “Take the child and his mother and flee to ܡܨܪܝܢ.”
“From ܡܨܪܝܢ I called my son.”
Joseph made ruler over ܡܨܪܝܢ.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s gentilic (ܡܨܪܝܐ), where the Greek has Αἰγύπτιος.

senses.definition: A person of Egypt; the Egyptians as a people.

evidence.note: Moses avenged the oppressed man and struck the ܡܨܪܝܐ.
“Are you not that ܡܨܪܝܐ who …?”

cognates.note: The same name in Arabic, singular like מָצוֹר. Lane’s article notes that the word, masculine or feminine, is used as the name of the metropolis of Egypt and of Egypt itself. Arabic ṣ (ص), not ḍ (ض) or ẓ (ظ), stands behind צ.

The Assyrian and Babylonian name of Egypt, written with the determinative for a land (KUR mu-ṣur, KUR mi-iṣ-ri). Muṣur has the vowels of מָצוֹר; the Oracc glossary vendored here lists common nouns only, so the place name is cited from Wiktionary until a cuneiform source is added.
Ugaritic has the same final -m as Hebrew מִצְרַיִם, and ṣ, not ẓ.
Jewish Aramaic of the Targums: the gentilic for Hebrew מִצְרִי (Targ. Onkelos Gen 39:1, 2, 5, of Potiphar; Exo 2:11; plural Gen 43:32; feminine Gen 16:3, Exo 1:19), and Egypt itself as מצרין.

evidence.note: Targ. Gen. 39:1, 2, 5; Targ. O. Ex. 2:11; pl. Targ. Gen. 43:32; fem. ib. 16:3; Targ. Ex. 1:19.

cognates.gloss: partition, boundary between two lands; a great town; (form II) make a town a boundary, found a city
cognates.note: Lane’s sources give miṣr as “a partition, barrier … between two things” and “limit, or boundary, between two lands”, and hence “a great town”, the seat of government of a province; the dual al-miṣrān names the two garrison cities Kufa and Basra. If this is the root of the name, Egypt is “the bounded land” or “the march”; nothing in scripture shows it, so it is recorded as possible.
Common Akkadian noun (over 1,500 attestations in Oracc), the same consonants and sense as Arabic miṣr “boundary”. Like that word it is a lead to the root of the name, not shown to be it.

evidence.locator: armep x000047790, miṣru [border] N (meanings: (an ornament) band, border, territory)

doctrine.statement: Yahweh names himself to Israel as the God “who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slaves” before he gives a single commandment (Exo 20:2), and the law repeats it as its ground: be holy, for I brought you up from Egypt to be your God (Lev 11:45); love the stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt (Lev 19:34); they are my servants, whom I brought out of Egypt, and shall not be sold as slaves (Lev 25:42, 55); keep the sabbath, remembering you were a slave in Egypt (Deu 5:15). The feasts keep the deliverance in memory, the booths of Lev 23 among them: “that your generations may know that I made the sons of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Lev 23:43; Exo 12:17; 23:15). From the verses: Israel’s obedience is the answer to a redemption already done; they belong to Yahweh because he bought them out of bondage.

Yahweh calls Israel “my son, my firstborn” and demands that Pharaoh let him go (Exo 4:22–23); Hosea looks back on it: “when Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos 11:1). Matthew writes that Jesus was taken to Egypt and brought back, “that it might be fulfilled … Out of Egypt I called my son” (Mat 2:13–15), and Hebrews says Moses counted “the reproach of the Christ” greater riches than the treasures of Egypt and left it by faith (Heb 11:26–27). From the verses: the nation’s exodus is the pattern of the Son of God’s own life; what Israel was called to be as God’s son, Jesus is.

Israel in the wilderness wanted to go back to Egypt (Num 14:3–4), and Stephen says the fathers “in their hearts turned back to Egypt” (Act 7:39). The law forbids the king to send the people back there for horses (Deu 17:16), the prophets condemn going down to Egypt for help, “for Egypt is man and not God” (Isa 31:1, 3), and the covenant’s last curse is to be taken back to Egypt in ships and sold (Deu 28:68; Hos 8:13). Jude warns that the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterwards destroyed those who did not believe (Jud 1:5; Heb 3:16–19), and Revelation calls the city “where also our Lord was crucified” spiritually Sodom and Egypt (Rev 11:8). From the verses: Egypt stands for the bondage God redeems from; trusting it or longing for it undoes the deliverance, and those brought out can still perish for unbelief.

Isaiah foretells an altar to Yahweh in the midst of the land of Egypt, Egypt crying to Yahweh and being sent a saviour, Egypt knowing Yahweh and serving him with sacrifice and offering, and Yahweh blessing it: “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance” (Isa 19:19–25). Zechariah, in the day when Yahweh is king over all the earth (Zec 14:9), says that all who are left of the nations will go up year by year to Jerusalem to worship the King and to keep the feast of booths, and names the family of Egypt as liable to the plague if it does not go up (Zec 14:16–19). From the verses: when Christ reigns from Jerusalem, Egypt, the house of Israel’s bondage, will itself worship Yahweh, and will keep the very feast that remembers Israel’s coming out of it (Lev 23:43).

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Leviticus 23 (מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם, Lev 23:43); the root does not occur in Numbers 10. Root key מצר, as the database keys it (BDB m.df.aa “√ of following”). Words: m.df.ab מִצְרַיִם, m.df.ad מִצְרִי (the corpus puts both keys on most tokens of מִצְרַיִם, so lexicon-support counts several hundred uses for מִצְרִי), m.df.ac מָצוֹר with the cross-reference m.dc.al (no tokens). m.df.ac’s fourteen tokens also carry r.bk.ab (מָצוֹר “siege” under צור, in tsur.json, whose note hands m.df.ac to this root); only 2Ki 19:24, Isa 19:6, 37:25 and Mic 7:12 (twice) are Egypt. The Septuagint renders these as “siege” (περιοχή, 2Ki 19:24) or not at all, so no Greek is given for מָצוֹר. Left out as other roots, though the database files them under מצר (they follow it in BDB’s sequence of מ words): מַקֵּל “rod, staff” (m.df.ar, 18 tokens; root מקל), the places Makkedah (m.df.aj) and Makaz (m.df.az), and the Benjamite Mikloth (m.df.as). Not here: מֵצַר “strait, distress” (Psa 116:3; 118:5; Lam 1:3), which scripture uses of narrowness and the corpus files under צרר; later Hebrew and Jewish Aramaic מֵצַר “balk, boundary between fields” (Jastrow M02356) may tie in with Arabic miṣr “boundary” and is a lead for a future צרר/מצר review. Names: Mizraim son of Ham is a TIPNR person (Egypt@Gen.10.6) but has no name entry, as the task named none; Egypt the place cannot have one. Leads not followed: Phoenician mṣrm (Krahmalkov, not checked by page); Assyrian “Meṣirānu” horses (Oracc meṣirānu, “designation of horse”, possibly “Egyptian”, cf. Deu 17:16; 1Ki 10:28); the Egyptian name of the land, km.t, is unrelated and not recorded.
